_meta.description: State unclaimed property programs and their finder/locator law posture. Powers /states/ pages, the search plan, and internal compliance checks.
_meta.verifyNote: Every searchUrl is link-checked by build/qa.js. Finder-law fields are research summaries for internal planning, NOT legal advice — confirm with counsel before charging fees in any state.
sources: State treasury / comptroller / revenue department official sites
unclaimed.org (National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators)

_excludedStatesNote: Add two-letter codes here to withhold service from a state (e.g. ["CA"]). Excluded states are dropped from page generation and flagged in the UI. Leave empty to serve all states.

states.name: California

finderLaw.notes: California limits finder fees and restricts agreements made before the property has been held for a set period. Confirm current Civil Code requirements before charging.

highlights: The State Controller holds billions of dollars in unclaimed property, among the largest pools in the country.
California property is held indefinitely — there is no deadline to claim what is yours.

states.name: Texas

finderLaw.notes: Texas caps recovery-agreement fees and restricts agreements soon after property is reported. Verify Property Code requirements before charging.

highlights: Administered by the Comptroller rather than a treasurer — a common point of confusion.
Texas holds unclaimed property indefinitely until claimed by the rightful owner.

states.name: Florida
states.office: Florida Department of Financial Services, Division of Unclaimed Property

finderLaw.notes: Florida requires finders to be registered and voids agreements made within 12 months of the property being reported, or within 90 days of a state notification attempt.

highlights: Branded as Florida Treasure Hunt and run by the Department of Financial Services.
Florida has among the stricter finder rules — registration and a 12-month agreement bar.

states.name: New York
states.program: New York Office of Unclaimed Funds

finderLaw.notes: New York requires Approved Personal Locating Service Providers (APLSP) to register with the Comptroller and follow prescribed agreement terms.

highlights: New York runs a formal Approved Personal Locating Service Provider program for finders.
The Comptroller returns millions of dollars in unclaimed funds each year.

states.name: Pennsylvania

finderLaw.notes: Pennsylvania Treasury certifies Finders. Assisting a claimant for a fee without certification is prohibited.

highlights: Pennsylvania Treasury operates a formal Finder certification program.
Fees are capped at 15% of the value recovered.

states.name: Illinois

finderLaw.notes: Illinois restricts fee agreements within a period after property is delivered to the Treasurer. Confirm RUUPA provisions before charging.

highlights: Branded I-Cash and run by the Illinois State Treasurer.
Illinois has returned record sums in recent years through automated claim matching.

states.name: Ohio
states.office: Ohio Department of Commerce, Division of Unclaimed Funds

finderLaw.notes: Ohio limits finder fees and restricts early agreements. Verify Revised Code provisions before charging.

highlights: Administered by the Department of Commerce rather than a treasurer.
Ohio holds unclaimed funds indefinitely with no claim deadline.

states.name: Georgia

finderLaw.notes: Georgia caps finder compensation and restricts agreements soon after property is reported.

highlights: Run by the Department of Revenue — not the treasurer, which trips up many searchers.
Georgia uses a 5-year dormancy period for many property types.

states.name: North Carolina
states.office: North Carolina Department of State Treasurer

finderLaw.notes: North Carolina requires annual Property Finder registration ($100/yr) and caps fees at the lesser of $1,000 or 20%. Non-compliant agreements are void and unenforceable.

highlights: Requires annual registration for anyone assisting claimants for a fee.
Fee cap is the lesser of $1,000 or 20% — one of the tightest in the country.

states.name: Michigan

finderLaw.notes: Michigan requires locators to register with the Department (registration fee applies, renewable every 4 years). No statutory percentage cap, but agreement requirements apply.

highlights: Locators must register with the Department of Treasury before assisting claimants for a fee.
Michigan holds unclaimed property indefinitely.
